#1057. AI is turbocharging cyberattacks — can computer scientists catch up?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

David Adam is a journalist based near London and author of The Man Who Couldn’t Stop (2014) and The Genius Within (2018).

Artificial intelligence systems are transforming the way software vulnerabilities are discovered.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.

At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.

Although probably unrelated, these incidents highlight a broader transformation in cybersecurity, say researchers. Artificial intelligence is changing how software vulnerabilities are discovered, allowing both attackers and security specialists to examine vast quantities of computer code at unprecedented speed.

“I think vulnerability discovery without AI is basically dead,” says Steven Murdoch, a computer security researcher at University College London. Researchers in the field who don’t use the technology now risk falling behind, he says.

AI can find weaknesses in software much faster than humans can, giving attackers time to exploit vulnerabilities before organizations can fix them. Researchers now want to understand how thoroughly AI can check software for security flaws, and whether it could introduce new weaknesses.

Agentic systems help attackers identify security vulnerabilities more rapidly and systematically. While hackers previously had to spend hours inspecting websites and probing software for weaknesses that offered unauthorized access to networks, AI agents use automated tools that can search millions of lines of computer code.

Google has reported that attackers have already used agentic AI to examine software updates, identify the security problems they address, and then find ways to exploit them.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects

“For me, it's about the scale,” says Daniel Gardham, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of Surrey. AI tends to find the same kinds of weaknesses as human hackers, but it makes it easier for people with limited technical expertise to break into systems.

“They can set an AI agent off and come back in 20 minutes and have dozens of results already,” he says.

Even with AI, most security breaches still involve human failure, he says, such as weak passwords (a common problem with Europe’s supermarket freezers was that passwords were defaults such as ‘admin’ or ‘12345’) or clicking on links from unfamiliar sources. AI-crafted messages can make such phishing messages more convincing and so more likely to succeed. They can draw on publicly available information to personalize fraudulent communications and make them appear authentic

Murdoch says AI is particularly good at discovering familiar kinds of software flaws, even if the most accomplished human researchers remain better at finding entirely new types of weakness. “They don't need to sleep,” he says. “You can happily work a hundred of them in parallel.”

These capabilities of AI helped discover security flaws in Java and PHP software, two programming languages that build cross-platform software and websites. In the Java case, for example, AI identified circumstances that could allow an attacker to corrupt computer memory. But Murdoch says the significance of the issue has been exaggerated.

The Java vulnerability, he says: “Is a real problem, but it’s not one of the top ten vulnerabilities this year or probably even this week.”

Just like hackers, cybersecurity researchers are using AI tools to quickly and efficiently find weaknesses in computer systems. Murdoch says this has become increasingly important to vulnerability researchers, who can now examine much larger quantities of software and work out how to patch up the defences where necessary. Researchers are also developing AI agents that can detect and repair vulnerabilities automatically.

When security researchers uncover a weakness, they typically notify the software developer privately, allowing engineers to prepare a remedy before publishing details of the problem.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

Murdoch says the use of AI in cyber security has shortened the time window between public disclosure and attempted exploitation – from several weeks, to just a few days.

Rushing an update can bring its own problems. A software patch can interfere with other programs and cause the sort of outage that organisations are trying to avoid.

“The life for the defenders who are trying to fix things has become significantly harder,” Murdoch says.

It’s unlikely that the recent tech outages were connected as large-scale cyber-attack, says Murdoch. The most prominent disruptions, he says, are likely technical malfunctions rather than anything more sinister.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

#1055. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition.  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

England want to host the Nations League, but things are never easy hosting international football in this country

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Football Association has registered interest in England hosting the Nations League finals.

On Sunday, the Three Lions booked their place as one of the top seeds in the newly expanded quarter-finals of the competition, beating world champions Spain to set up a clash against a second seed in March.

And England could well be playing a semi on home soil, if the FA has anything to do with it.

According to Sami Mokbel of the BBC, England, Spain and France have all contacted UEFA, expressing their desire to host the final four games of next summer's Nations League competition.

The competition began in 2019, with the inaugural finals both hosted and ultimately won by Portugal, before heading to Italy (2021), the Netherlands (2023), and, most recently, Germany (2025).

England will face one of Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in the last eight of the competition – and could well become the first host of the finals not to reach the final four, given the new format of the competition.

So far, the only publically announced events at Wembley this June are two concerts from Newcastle United fan, Sam Fender, though these are scheduled to take place after the Nations League is due to be played.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the FA would welcome the opportunity to host a mini-tournament with the European Championship coming to the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland in 2028 – with other venues in consideration for hosting duties next summer.

While the Etihad Stadium is booked for much of June for Oasis's Live '27 tour, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium is, so far, free to host, with cult noughties emo band Fall Out Boy and stadium rock veterans U2 booked either side of when the semi-finals would take place.

The Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, meanwhile, could well host its first major internationals.

This isn't a new conundrum for the FA to solve, with the Community Shield recently affected by Wembley's commitments beyond football.

This summer, the season's curtain-raiser was held in Cardiff at the Millennium Stadium, while 2022 saw Erling Haaland make his Manchester City debut at the King Power Stadium in the fixture.

England will play home and away in the next international break in the Nations League quarter.

#1053. Thomas Frank hints there is more to tell from disastrous Spurs reign as he starts life at Palace

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Frank is back in the dugout with Crystal Palace, his first job since being sacked by Tottenham at the beginning of the year

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank has teased that there is more to the story of his torrid time at Tottenham he will be willing to tell once he has steered Crystal Palace back on course.

The 53-year-old was prepared for plenty of questions about his past employers when he was unveiled to the media on Thursday afternoon ahead of Saturday’s trip to Coventry, acknowledging “I know today is a lot about me”.

The Danish boss helped stabilise Brentford in the Premier League, and was nominated for the league’s Manager of the Year award while with the Bees, but could not replicate the same success at Spurs and was sacked after just under eight months in charge.

“It’s something I’ve… maybe one day I’ll tell a little bit more about it,” said Frank, whose deal through June 2029 was announced on Monday.

“I understand why it’s also interesting. I think it’s more about Palace in general today. What can I say? I always said the day I got sacked, I’ll have time to travel, so I think I was relatively quick over it.

“But of course you want success, and I’m competitive, so I think that answer probably demands a little bit more time, which I am happy to do one day.”

For now, Frank – who spent his time off in Japan, Australia and Denmark – has to figure out what to do with a side resuming their Premier League season in last place, while also balancing a Europa League campaign that continues next Thursday at home against Real Sociedad.

On Thursday, Palace confirmed two additions to the new boss’ backroom staff, with Justin Cochrane joining as first-team coach and Chris Haslam as fitness and athletic performance coach.

Cochrane worked with Frank at both Brentford and Tottenham, and is currently part of Thomas Tuchel’s England set-up, while Haslam was previously the head of athletic performance at Frank’s former employers Brentford, and also works as a fitness coach with the Danish FA.

Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva was also confirmed as part of Frank’s team on Friday morning, with existing staff Paddy McCarthy, the assistant manager, and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy retained.

Frank is a firm believer that “culture is everything”, and boils down his philosophy to a “no dickheads” approach to crafting a cohesive, successful environment.

Asked about claims that his success at Brentford had more to do with the model, he replied: “Let’s put it this way: I think I was pretty important in terms of building that model.”

He has no qualms about what he has witnessed so far from a squad he is still getting to know as many have recently returned from international duty.

Frank added: “The players were buzzing. That told me, ‘Oh, that’s good. They like to be together’. That’s very important, because it’s been tough times until now.

“Hopefully we can just continue, but there will also be ups and downs in games and whatever, and that’s why we need each other.”

#1051. Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football

The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," Ronaldo said.

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.

He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.

"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.

"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it."

He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.

The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.

Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

Lee Carsley is speaking very highly of him for a long time now. He is the captain of the U21s, the stand-out player. I think the door should always be open for the pathway, the door should always be open for special performers over a long period of time and that is what Jobe has done.

He has found his way and his rhythm with Dortmund who have had an excellent start to the season. He is a regular starter there and there is an opportunity because Myles is suspended for the Croatia game.

Jobe comes through the pathway and on his own merit and deserves to make an impression for us. That’s why we are delighted he is with us in camp and we can see what he can do for us.

He misses too many opportunities to impress. The trust is for the players who are in camp. It is not personal and we will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset to come in and play, but the players in camp did an amazing job.

It’s enough No10s and we stick to the guys who were in camp. We were happy with the last two-and-a-half weeks we had together. He covers all eventualities because Josh can play all four positions. That’s basically the reason.

Jude has previously spoken about his dream to play in the same England team as his brother, who is two years younger than him and has also followed his path by playing for Dortmund. Jobe moved there from Sunderland at the start of last season and finished his first campaign in Bundesliga as a regular starter.

“We’ve played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life, that would mean more than any of the trophies, nothing would even get close to that. Nothing,” said Jude two years ago.

Jobe Bellingham’s call-up for the England squad is ahead of Everton’s Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, who has been in eye-catching form for Everton. It also shows that Tuchel is thinking of the future, with Jordan Henderson not picked despite his presence in the World Cup squad.

England checked with Chelsea and were told that Palmer was fit for international duty if selected. “Load management” not an issue this time, then.

He is doing well. The reason why he has been left out, I don’t know. But we are happy with Phil. It is my duty to help him and slowly, slowly he will be back to his best. We are very happy with Phil.

And the message is plain: miss a camp for reasons with which he does not agree and pay the price.

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

#1049. Drone operator deletes footage of Mauricio Pochettino’s first Man Utd training session and issues apology

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The drone operator said he made a ‘total error of judgement’ and insisted he was not working on behalf of any club

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A drone operator ​who filmed Manchester United's training session this week has apologised for what he called a "total error of judgment" and removed the footage from ⁠his YouTube channel.

The footage, filmed at United's Carrington training ground during new manager Mauricio Pochettino's first training session on Thursday, was uploaded online under the username "CC OVERVIEW".

In a statement ⁠posted on his YouTube channel ​on ⁠Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight was legal under drone regulations, filming ⁠the session had been "unethical".

“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he wrote.

“I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown.”

The operator added that he had wrongly assumed that the training session would be open to various media outlets. Pochettino’s first session was closed to the press.

“I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” he said.

"I would also like to state that Liverpool Football Club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday. The video has been removed from my channel.

“I have spent the past four years building up my YouTube channel and were well regarded in the fields I film and would now like to get back to building up my damaged reputation and making well received responsible videos.”

The footage has nevertheless been shared across social media and garnered millions of views. United have not commented on the matter.

United have a strict no drones policy and have signs around Carrington warning that anyone caught using a drone "will be reported for prosecution and subject to civil action".

Pochettino arrived from ‌the US men's national team ⁠this week after United sacked Michael Carrick, ⁠and faces an immediate test with a trip to Liverpool on ‌Sunday.

United are languishing 18th in the league table after winning just one of their 10 games, while Liverpool sit fourth.

#1047. England handed suspended supporter ban for discriminatory chanting in Spain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The punishment reportedly relates to anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England have been handed a suspended ban for away supporters as a result of “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” by fans during Sunday’s 3-2 win over Spain in Madrid.

The ban, which would apply to one match, is suspended for a period of two years, meaning any similar offence during that period would enforce it.

The FA has also been fined €15,000 (£12,600).

The punishment reportedly relates to anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting which was heard in the Spanish capital.

"We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police, who attend all England home and away matches, to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action," an FA spokesperson said.

England fans’ group Free Lions has condemned the offensive chanting, writing in a statement: “We are extremely disappointed to find that England fans face the possibility of an away ban as a result of chants by a section of supporters.

“There is no place for offensive chants aimed at religious figures. The time for these chants is over. No tit-for-tat arguments. No excuses.

“The behaviour and reputation of England supporters abroad has improved significantly over the years but these chants undermine that progress.”

The build-up to the match was overshadowed by concerns of racist chanting from Spain fans, with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel, who insisted he didn’t expect any incidents, then fumed at how his words were apparently “twisted” as Spain manager Luis de la Fuente issued a firm response to the German.

"What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism,” De la Fuente said.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten record at the weekend, taking a 3-0 lead through Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White but then hanging on after a red card for Elliot Anderson.

#1045. Jayden Bogle receives threats and racist abuse after Leeds’ win over Tottenham

Leeds and the Premier League are launching an investigation into racist abuse and threats sent to Jayden Bogle’s family.

Bogle escaped a red card in the win over Tottenham after injuring Mathys Tel, with the Leeds full-back receiving the threats via social media.

Should Jason Bogle have seen red for this challenge? 🟥👀 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/fuK42Okkcz

His club have revealed they are looking to identify those who sent messages to the 26-year-old, whose family were threatened in one of the posts seen by Telegraph Sport after the 1-0 victory.

Leeds say they are “appalled at the disgusting, racist social-media abuse Jayden Bogle suffered” and will push for punishments to be taken.

The club added in a statement: “Leeds United condemns this behaviour in the strongest possible terms. There is no place for racism in football or society.

“The club will work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify the individuals and push for the strongest possible action to be taken against them.

“Jayden has the full and unconditional support of the club and his team-mates, and we all stand with him at this time. Nobody should ever be subjected to racist abuse.”

Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, described Bogle as the “softest player” in the Premier League who would never try to hurt an opponent.

Referee John Brooks did not issue a yellow card, with VAR Tony Harrington sticking with the on-field decision.

“I’m confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge,” Harrington was quoted on the big screen at Elland Road.

Tottenham will make a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to send off Bogle.

“I haven’t watched the scenes back so I can’t give you a clear opinion, out of the game it looked a handball but the scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench and it looked a very unlucky coming together,” Farke said.

“Fingers crossed for Mathys that he is back soon, but it looked like there was not much speed in this action, but Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the country, he would never injure or foul a player on purpose because he is such a fair character.”

Tottenham Hotspur’s purple patch of form ended with a worrying loss. Wearing their “Spurple” kit for the first time, Roberto De Zerbi highlighted a lack of character and personality from his players and refused to blame the defeat on referee John Brooks’s decision not to dismiss Jayden Bogle for leaving one of his players injured.

Spurs’ away strip is based on a 1990s design, but this performance was more Christian Gross than Jürgen Klinsmann or David Ginola. Leeds United created the better chances and eventually broke through with 11 minutes remaining when their substitutes combined for Noah Okafor to score the winning goal.

Noah Okafor came off the bench and broke the deadlock just minutes later ⛓️‍💥 What a finish 🎯 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/pnbTQM1YpM

After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move Spurs into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

Bogle trod on his opponent’s foot before clattering into his knee, forcing the French forward off a few minutes later. “I know that Jayden doesn’t foul out of bad intentions, he is not a nasty player and is one of the softest players in the whole league,” Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said. “I call him my butterfly.”

De Zerbi admitted the injury was “bad” and that Tel would now be scanned to determine the extent of the problem. The Spurs boss was upset that Pedro Porro was later booked for a similar challenge, while Bogle went unpunished – but he said the referee was not the cause of the defeat.

“I was surprised because in the same position in the second half there were two different fouls, the yellow card for Pedro Porro is not possible. I don’t know if it is a red card or not on Mathys Tel but the parameter of the referee was not good enough for this in both situations,” De Zerbi said.

Okafor was only on the pitch for 97 seconds before he finished off a move made by Farke’s replacements. Half-time substitute Melvin Bard sent a throw-in to Harry Wilson, who had also just come on and Okafor did the rest, bursting past Rodrigo Bentancur and planting his finish into the bottom corner. It meant the home fans were singing their “I Predict A Riot” winning anthem for just the second time this season.

For Leeds, moving into the top half will lift their own hopes of challenging for Europe, such is the congested mid-table.

“For us it has been a difficult period, we are missing key players like Anton Stach, Noah, Dominic [Calvert-Lewin] has not had the easiest spell with several injury problems and it was important to show this unity and commitment to avoid all their individual quality to score goals and reduce them to very little,” Farke added.

Archie Gray will make his first appearance against his old club today after joining Spurs from Leeds in 2024. He was an unused sub in the two matches last season but is now an established part of this De Zerbi resurgence, starting all but two matches in the current campaign. Gray was named in the England Under-21 squad yesterday but is heading in the right direction for a senior call-up.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is starting for Leeds today, after doubts over a foot issue heading into the Elland Road fixture. He was named in the England squad yesterday, which suggested he was not ruled out of this clash against Spurs

Roberto De Zerbi has kept a settled team as he looks to make it four Premier League wins in a row. Dominic Solanke is dropped to the bench in his only change, with Pedro Porro coming in – so it may be Omar Marmoush playing as a central forward.

There are many processes in [Tottenham’s] build-up. You need players to interpret this and the legs to cover the centre of the game. It is always complicated [tactically against a De Zerbi team], very dominant in possession. You have to find solutions to be competitive in this area.

The most important thing is what happens on the pitch but [we have bought] Sean [in because of the] tactical aspect. He is sop smart, has experience and also the legs to compete. It’s necessary to have a third midfielder on the pitch to control their processes. On the other hand he is sharp on the offensive actions, many times. Lukas [Nmecha] brings the greediness, physicality and can take the attention off Dominic. he has been very sharp in training, scoring many goals and for that he has the chance to shine today.

Dominic is a key player and thank God he was able to join us in team training yesterday. Overall he is in a good position.

You will always have spells in the Premier League when you cannot convert good performances into results or when you can’t score many goals. We are struggling with injuries for key players in our attack – Noah Okafor, Anton Stach – but hopefully we have also turned the corner.

The pre-season, it was clear [he is] a special talent. You recognise the special talent immediately and he doesn’t need to show something special, you understand? Everything that he does and he is one of the special talents.

The next step he has to enjoy, he has to follow the older players, the players with more experience like [Andrew] Robertson, [James] Maddison, Ben Davies and to find the time to play.

It is my responsibility because when you manage young players and sucho big talents like Luca, it is a bigger responsibility for me.

He has to be ready when he goes on the pitch. I think it [does] not depend on the result, he can play from the beginning. Before the Chelsea game, I thought to play with him in the first XI, but in the end you have to find the right moment and for them also.

I think the age is not so important. The most important is the quality, personality, the behaviour on the pitch and the qualities. And Luca has all of these qualities.

Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

Tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

#1044. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

#1043. Renee Slegers left wanting more as Arsenal’s Champions League hopes dented by superior Lyon

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Arsenal 0-2 Lyon: Defeat at Borehamwood dented the Gunners’ hopes of direct qualification for the Champions League quarter-finals

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal head coach Renee Slegers admitted her side had been outmuscled by a clinical Lyon side after a 2-0 defeat at Borehamwood dented hopes of direct qualification for the Champions League quarter-finals.

Lyon were yet to concede a goal in Europe this season and had won all of their nine domestic league matches so far.

The French side made the most of a bright start to take a 24th-minute lead through Jule Brand, and should have gone into half-time with a bigger advantaged but Marie-Antoinette Katoto – top scorer in the Champions League this season with seven goals – blazed over from six yards.

Although Arsenal were improved early in the second half, with Caitlin Foord stretching Lyon down the flanks, clear chances were still hard to come by.

Lyon added a second against the run of play in the 57th minute when Melchie Dumornay drilled a shot into the top corner following another blistering counter attack.

“It was a tough game, it was a challenge,” Slegers said, quoted on the Arsenal club website.

“Especially the first half, also parts of the second half, the game becomes what they are good at, it was physical, it was fast. They are clinical with their moments, you see the quality they have.

“The second half, we dominated the game better, in possession, spent more time in their half, (but) still didn’t create clear cut chances.”

Arsenal – who had battled to a 1-1 draw at holders Barcelona last time out – slipped to a first European defeat this season and ended the night in eighth place.

Lyon sit joint top with Barcelona on 13 points and already assured of a place in the quarter-finals ahead of the final round of league stage games.

Arsenal will be away to Inter Milan and could yet still avoid having to go into the play-off round if other results also go their way.

“It is the three points in Milan, that is everything we can control,” Slegers said. “That is what we go for, and then we will see what the other teams do.”

#1041. The last golden era of the Premier League is long gone: Why 2004-16 was the best of the Barclays

With the English top-flight a state of flux right now, it's not hard to yearn for years gone by.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.

The bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before. Is there a title race? Who’s going down? What is real? Does any of this mean anything? Throw in the continued abomination that is VAR and more, and it’s all just a bit bleak.

So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.

While football didn’t start in 1992, the Premier League did and by the early-to-mid 2000s, it was reaching its apex as the blood and thunder of decades prior fused with the new-found flair and panache to create a near-perfect concoction.

The current state of the English top-flight can be traced all the way back to the summer of 2003 with Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea. It was the moment the horse bolted and nothing has been the same since.

However, at the time, it was all just a little bit exciting and things really picked up 12 months later when Jose Mourinho landed in West London, rightly claiming to be the “Special One”. The reigning European Cup winner was joined by Rafael Benitez, who came to Liverpool after incredible success with Valencia.

Suddenly, Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger were no longer the only gunslingers in town. The “Big Two” quickly became the “Big Four” as Mourinho romped to the league title - breaking numerous records - and Benitez amazingly won the Champions League. Istanbul and all that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The two Iberians changed so much in the English game. From how to set up a side to how to win the title - 4-4-2 and peaking after Christmas being swapped out for 4-3-3 and rapid-fast starts.

Liverpool’s fifth European Cup was significant for numerous reasons. It was their first in 21 years but also the first final featuring an English side in the 21st century. They had beaten Chelsea to get there, starting both an incredible rivalry between the clubs and managers, and a golden age for the Premier League.

Over the next four years, all of the then-”Big Four” made finals and there were three semi-finalists in every season from 06/07 to 08/09. The peak came in 2008 when each was knocked out by another with United eventually toppling Chelsea in the first all-English final in Moscow. In one of the odder paradoxes, England failed to qualify for the European Championships that summer.

Fergie’s empire had struck back with Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney at the forefront of it. In an era of elite pairings, there was no finer. Ronaldo’s Ballon d’Or win confirmed his status as the best player in the world, and the Premier League as truly the best league.

It was also a time of far less financial disparity with the rest of Europe, Milan and Inter lifting the Champions League in 2007 and 2010 respectively. Things would soon change and not for the better.

While the big boys competed for the biggest trophies, there were plenty of brilliant stories elsewhere. Harry Redknapp’s Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008, setting the tone for Wigan five years later in epic fashion against City months on from Swansea claiming the League Cup. Only Crystal Palace's success in 2025 has been comparable since.

Throw in Big Sam’s Bolton, Blackburn, Stoke, Hull and others and it was the last definitive age of the cult teams and cult heroes, or as they’ve become better known - The Barclaysmen. With the overload of data nowadays, another Michu-like madness feels further away than ever.

Abu Dhabi’s takeover of City in 2008 is the obvious place to pinpoint the beginning of the end, but Mourinho’s first Chelsea exit a year prior and Ronaldo’s first from United a year after moved the centre of attention from England to Spain.

While European success faded - a fate-like Chelsea were the only winners from 2008 to 2019 - there were still memorable domestic moments, two of which unfortunately led to City winning their first pair of Premier League titles. Agueroooooo and Gerrard’s slip may be rendered utterly irrelevant soon but the memories won’t. It was peak Premier League.

As was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last dance in 2013 and Leicester’s miracle title win in 2016, which will never be topped as the greatest achievement in the history of English football. That it came either side of Chelsea’s crooked titles and prior to City’s dodgy dominance makes it all the more appropriate as the ending of the last great era. And that goes for both in football and the world itself.

While the on-field action of the last decade may feel fraudulent, how we now consume football is also a far cry from those halcyon Barclays days.

Streaming was not yet a thing in 2004. Sky Sports was in its pomp. Super Sunday actually lived up to its billing as appointment viewing.

Influencers and content creators had not yet taken over. Gary Neville went past his winger on the overlap rather than host it. Social media was still fun for the most part.

We had Soccer AM and Goals on Sunday, Gillette Soccer Saturday and Match of the Day at elite levels, and even room for shows like Wayne Rooney’s Street Striker and Football’s Next Star.

Nostalgia is a helluva drug, but as Independent Panels decide the fate of English football past, present and future, it’s near-impossible to dispute that, like so much of entertainment, we had it so much better before.

One day, the pendulum will hopefully swing back in our favour but, for now, a rewatch of Premier League Years on Sky may be in order.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV shows and attempting to play tennis.

#1040. Arsenal handed William Saliba boost as Mikel Arteta gives Bukayo Saka injury update

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Bukayo Saka faces a longer spell on the sidelines but there was positive news for long-term absentee William Saliba

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal winger Bukayo Saka is facing another month on the sidelines as he continues to recover from a thigh injury, taking his absence to eight weeks.

Saka picked up the injury early in a Champions League game against Bayern Munich on 21 October.

Manager Mikel Arteta issued the update at a press conference ahead of the Premier League’s return, with Arsenal heading to Newcastle for their first game since the international break.

Arteta said Saka had undergone more tests on the issue and was “evolving really well”.

He said: “It looks like it’s going to be an eight-week injury, more or less, so I think it’s four at the moment. Still a while before he's back with the team.”

Arsenal will also be missing midfielder Martin Zubimendi for a “few weeks” after he picked up a hamstring injury with Spain during the Nations League break, but the Gunners were handed a boost with centre-back William Saliba finally available for selection after a lengthy absence.

The Frenchman has been struggling with a back injury which he was managing at the end of the 2025-26 campaign, and it brought his World Cup to a premature end as he was forced off half an hour into France’s semi-final defeat.

But he did not require surgery and after several months out, has now played two practice matches and is set to be included in the squad.

Arteta said: “He's ready. He's in a good condition. He played two games, one behind closed doors and one more official and he did really well and he's in good condition.

On Zubimendi, Arteta said: “He's out. Unfortunately he has a slight problem in his hamstring. He wasn't too concerned after the game but after the MRI scan showed there's an injury there and he's going to be out for a few weeks.”

Arteta also responded to the idea that Fantasy Premier League (FPL) selections by top-flight players, staff and family members have contributed towards team news leaks in recent weeks.

He said: “It's a topic. This is the kind of things that are happening in our society right now and it's something new, we haven't dealt with it and we have to put new things in place.

“The confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and what you're trying to do and that should be kept as a huge secret. And we will take measures to make sure that doesn't happen.”
